explanations.bohemian-revolt--siege-of-pilsen--enable: The siege’s own article puts the two in that order and names the army: “The Siege of Pilsen, 19 September to 21 November 1618, was the first significant action of the Thirty Years’ War. Following the Bohemian Revolt, a Bohemian army under Ernst von Mansfeld captured Plzeň.” The army that took the city is the revolt’s own, which is why this is `enabled` rather than `caused`: the article says the revolt put that force in the field, not that it decided the siege. `probable`, on one lead, and rule 22 refuses `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation.
explanations.bohemian-revolt--thirty-years-war--cause: The revolt’s own article states it in the first sentence: it was “an uprising of the Bohemian estates against the rule of the Habsburg dynasty that began the Thirty Years’ War”. The same lead says the defeat at White Mountain “expanded the scope of the Thirty Years’ War by drawing Denmark and Sweden into it”, so the article treats the revolt as the thing the war grew out of and not merely as its first episode. The atlas already types a war’s opening action this way — Operation Rosary and the Falklands War, the Moncada attack and the Cuban Revolution — and this is that shape. It stays `probable`: one encyclopaedia lead reporting where the consensus sits is not a work arguing it, and rule 22 would refuse `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation in any case. That the revolt is also filed as part of the war is a separate statement; `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so the argument has to be made as an edge or not at all.
explanations.capture-of-bahia--dutch-brazil-1630-1654: The 1624 seizure of Salvador was the West India Company's first attempt on Brazil, and the colony of 1630 was the second one. The Dutch Brazil article, at revision 1375595876, puts both in the same design: "As part of the Groot Desseyn plan, admiral Jacob Willekens led a GWC force to Salvador in December 1623, which was then the capital of Brazil and the center of a captaincy famous for its sugarcane", and then, of the funds Piet Heyn took at Matanzas Bay in 1628, that they "provided the GWC the funds for another attempt to conquer Brazil at Pernambuco" — another attempt is an attempt after the first. The Capture of Bahia article names the same plan. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article makes the 1630 conquest the second try of one Company design, and does not say the first try brought the second about.
explanations.capture-of-bahia--recapture-of-bahia--re: The Capture of Bahia article closes its lead on the answer this edge names: "Although the Dutch intentions were reported to the Spanish, no preventive counter-action was taken until the Recapture of Bahia in 1625." The Recapture article opens with the same thing said from the other side: "The recapture of Bahia was a Spanish–Portuguese military expedition in 1625 to retake the city of Bahia in Brazil from the forces of the Dutch West India Company (WIC)." An expedition mounted to retake a city taken the year before is a reaction to the taking and not a consequence of it, so `reacted-to` and not `caused`. Probable, because both articles are read at one revision each and neither names a historian for the reading.
explanations.dutch-brazil-1630-1654--the-caribbean-su: This is the edge that makes the two chains one picture, and it is a transfer of a technique, a people and a supply chain rather than a resemblance. The cane that transformed Barbados came from Dutch Brazil in 1640; Colonel James Drax went to Pernambuco that year and bought a triple-roller mill and a set of copper cauldrons; the Sephardic families who had left Iberia for Dutch Brazil were, in the cited account, instrumental in the early success of the Barbadian industry; and Dutch traders supplied the equipment, the financing, the enslaved Africans and the shipping to Europe. What the West India Company had built at Recife it lost by 1654, and it had already been carried north.
explanations.dutch-portuguese-war--dutch-brazil-1630-: Dutch Brazil was the American theatre of this war and not an enterprise beside it. The war's article, at revision 1374150566, describes a conflict in which "the Dutch companies and fleet" were "invading Portuguese colonies in the Americas, Africa, and the East Indies"; the Dutch Brazil article dates the American half of that to the fleet of sixty-five ships under Hendrick Corneliszoon Loncq, which "gained control of Olinda by 16 February 1630, and Recife (the capital of Pernambuco) and António Vaz by March 3". `enabled` rather than `caused`: the war is what made a Company fleet in Brazilian waters possible, and the colony is one of the things that possibility was spent on. The atlas also files the colony under the war as a part of it; `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so the causal reading is written here or nowhere.
explanations.english-settlement-of-barbados-1627--the: The first ship to the settlement carried six enslaved Africans among sixty-odd settlers, and about forty enslaved Taíno were brought from Guyana to plant. The scale is the whole difference from what came after: before 1650 more than three quarters of the islands’ population was of European descent, and by 1680 the median Barbadian estate held sixty enslaved people. The colony is where the traffic landed; it is not why it grew.

Thirteen years separate the landing at Holetown from the cane that changed everything, and in those thirteen years Barbados was a tobacco colony of tenants working for a London merchant. That is the point of keeping the two records apart rather than writing one: the settlement is not the sugar revolution and did not contain it in embryo. What it supplied was an English island with cleared ground, a population and a proprietor — the thing Drax could bring a mill back to in 1640.
explanations.saint-domingue-and-the-french-sugar-colo: The revolution is the colony’s own structure coming apart. Ogé’s revolt of free men of colour in 1790 and the citizenship granted them in May 1791 set them against the slave owners and destabilised the colony; the rising of 21 August 1791 came out of that. Saint-Domingue was the most thoroughly enslaved place in the Caribbean and the richest, and the two facts are the same fact; what rose in 1791 was the majority the sugar economy had assembled.
explanations.the-atlantic-slave-trade-to-the-caribbea: A hundred and fifty years, and the weakest type. The traffic did not organise the rising and nothing about it made a successful revolution likely — the cited account calls it the only slave rebellion known to have founded a state free of slavery and ruled by former captives, which is a statement about how rarely this happened. What the traffic supplied was the demographic fact the revolution was made out of: an enslaved majority, overwhelmingly African-born, in a colony held by a small white population.

A separate claim from the one above and worth keeping separate. That edge says the islands created the demand; this one says the traffic already existed, in Dutch and Portuguese hands — Dutch traders were supplying Barbados with its enslaved labour as well as its equipment and its credit — and that a monopoly company granted by the crown was how England moved to carry its own. A monopoly is a claim on an existing trade, not the invention of one.

France got the western third of Hispaniola recognised at Ryswick in 1697 and made it the richest sugar colony in the Caribbean, which it could do because the Atlantic traffic was by then a going concern that a new colony could buy into rather than build. `enabled` and not `caused`: the traffic did not make France take Saint-Domingue, and the French had been on Tortuga and the western coast for decades before. What it made possible was the speed and the scale.

What struck in Jamaica at Christmas 1831 was the population the traffic had assembled: by the eighteenth century the sugar islands held three enslaved Africans for every planter, and the estates had grown from smallholdings into units of sixty and more. The weak type is right here. The traffic did not organise the strike — a Baptist minister did — and the atlas should not take the agency of the people who withdrew their labour and hand it to the thing that had been done to them. What it supplied is the demographic ground.

The most contested link either chain touches, and the reason `disputed` exists in this schema. The thesis is Eric Williams’s in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), stated by Carrington as: the slave trade and the sugar industry based on slavery led to the formation of capital in England which helped finance the Industrial Revolution. The plantations supplied 80 to 90 per cent of the sugar consumed in western Europe and Barbados alone out-traded every other English colony combined by 1660, so there is no argument about whether the profits were large; the argument is about what they did. The atlas marks the link rather than asserting it, and a reader who opens this edge gets the disagreement rather than a line drawn confidently through it.

The Cuban boom is the last chapter of the traffic this chain is centred on and not a new thing: Cuba kept slavery until October 1886, half a century after the British islands and two years before Brazil, and it kept importing while it could. `enabled` rather than `caused`, because the boom’s occasion was Haiti and its market was North American; what the traffic supplied was the only labour force the Cuban planters intended to use.
explanations.the-brazilian-gold-cycle--the-british-in: The flow is not in doubt and the mechanism is on the record. Eight hundred tonnes of gold were shipped officially from Minas to Portugal over the eighteenth century, and the cited account says what Lisbon did with it: paid for industrialised goods, textiles and weapons, from countries that had the industry Portugal lacked. The Methuen terms of 1703 had already guaranteed English textiles admission to Portugal at all times, whatever the political weather. What is disputed is the same thing that is disputed about Caribbean sugar — whether colonial windfalls of this kind financed British industrialisation or merely accompanied it — and the atlas will not settle from one side of it.
explanations.the-brazilian-gold-cycle--transfer-of-th: The reason given in the sources is logistical and is the whole of it: Rio de Janeiro lay closer to the mining region and gave the gold a harbour to leave from, so in 1763 the capital of the State of Brazil moved there from Salvador and the king’s representative began to be called Viceroy. The centre of gravity of the colony had already moved — by 1725 half the population lived in the south-east — and the capital followed it.

A court in flight goes somewhere that can keep it. The reason given for Brazil, in so many words, is that it was by then the richest and most developed of the Portuguese colonies, and what had made it so within living memory was the gold: eight hundred tonnes shipped over the century, half the population of the colony resettled into the south-east by 1725. The type is the weak one, and deliberately: the mines did not send the French army into Portugal. They are why the answer to the invasion could be a transatlantic capital rather than a surrender.
explanations.the-caribbean-sugar-revolution--royal-af: Twenty years after Drax brought the mill home, the restored Stuart crown chartered a company with a monopoly on all English trade with Africa, overseen by the king’s brother. It was chartered to look for gold on the Gambia and it went into people instead, and historians estimate it shipped more enslaved Africans to the Americas than any other company. The demand it turned to was the sugar islands’, and the turn is what the edge claims.
explanations.the-caribbean-sugar-revolution--the-atla: Sugar was a cash crop with economies of scale, grown most efficiently on large estates with many workers, and the sources say the plantations made extensive use of enslaved people for that reason. The proportions move together: three quarters of the islands European before 1650, three enslaved Africans to every planter after the cane. The causal claim is the strong one and is about magnitude — the traffic to the Caribbean existed before the sugar revolution and became the largest forced migration in history because of it.
